# Introduction
This notebook performs an exploratory data analysis (EDA) on lung cancer mortlity data in the United States, covering the years **2000 to 2019**.  
This data were downloaded from **https://ghdx.healthdata.org/record/ihme-data/us-lung-cancer-county-race-ethnicity-2000-2019**.
Our notebook explores patterns and disparities in lung cancer mortality across the United States from 2000 to 2019. The data we use originates from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study, in which the most recent published data is up to 2019. We chose not to incorporate other datasets because this source alone contains over 19 million records, which provides sufficient coverage for our analysis. We will begin by introducing the dataset and its key variables, then examine national trends on each variables, and finally investigate demographic and geographic disparities over time.

# Dataset and Motivation
Currently, there are more than 100 types of cancers around the world. Of all, lung cancer has been the first and most diagnosed cancer. It became a threat to public health worldwide. By 2020, there were nearly 2 million cases related to lung cancer deaths. (Tesfaw et al.). While screenings such as low-dose computed tomography can significantly reduce lung cancer mortality, access to these screenings remains unevenly distributed and often limited, especially for vulnerable populations. The barriers to screening include a lack of awareness about risk factors, financial constraints, and geographic limitations. Previous studies have shown that lung cancer outcomes are linked to comorbid conditions (e.g., hypertension, diabetes), as well as behavioral and environmental factors. Although disparities in cancer outcomes have been widely studied, there is limited literature examining how these disparities have evolved over time.

Our dataset includes these varaibles: year of observation, state, sex, age group, race, and the mortality rate (deaths per 100,000 residents). By analyzing these variables, we can track how lung cancer mortality has changed over time in the US, compare rates between men and women, examine differences among racial and age groups, and identify geographic patterns across states. This not only enable us to explore the national trends, but also disparities that may exist between different populations and regions, which ultimately helps inform targeted population and suggests public health strategies or interventions.

In summary, with the variables in our current dataset, we aim to address the following questions:
1. How have lung cancer mortality rates changed nationally over the past two decades?
2. What disparities exist across sex, age, and race?
3. How have these disparities shifted over time?


# Package Set Up
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(skimr)
library(GGally)
```

# Forming our Dataset
```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Combining all yearly CSV files together (all csv file have the exact same data structure, varied by year)
male_files <- list.files("data/male", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)
female_files <- list.files("data/female", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE, ignore.case = TRUE)

male_data <- male_files %>%
  map_dfr(~ read_csv(.x) %>% clean_names()) %>%
  mutate(sex_name = "Male")

female_data <- female_files %>%
  map_dfr(~ read_csv(.x) %>% clean_names()) %>%
  mutate(sex_name = "Female")

lung_cancer_df <- bind_rows(male_data, female_data)
```

# Quick Overview

```{r}
glimpse(lung_cancer_df)
```
Our dataset contains over 16 million rows and 19 columns. We will clean the data to extract the variables relevant to our analysis and rename them to be more descriptive. The val column contains our primary variable of interest: the mortality rate.

## Data Preprocessing
Before starting our analysis, we performed data preprocessing to ensure the dataset was organized and clean. The mortality rate was normalized to improve visualization, state names were extracted to create a new state variable, and missing values were removed.
```{r}
# Clean and Structure Data
lung_clean <- lung_cancer_df %>%
  mutate(
    state = str_extract(location_name, "(?<=\\().+?(?=\\))"),
    state = if_else(is.na(state), location_name, state),
    
    # Normalize death rate per 100,000 population
    mortality_rate = val * 100000,
    lower_ci = lower * 100000,
    upper_ci = upper * 100000
  ) %>%
  select(
    year,
    state,
    sex = sex_name,
    age_group = age_name,
    race = race_name,
    mortality_rate,
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(mortality_rate), state != "United States of America")

# Missing Values Check
colSums(is.na(lung_clean))
unique(lung_clean$state)
```

After cleaning, the new dataset for our analysis contains approximately 9 million rows and 8 columns.
```{r}
# Preview of Cleaned Data
glimpse(lung_clean)
```

# National Trends Over Time
## 1. Overall Mortality Rate (2000–2019)
Using the cleaned data, we examine how has morality rate change over years. We created a line plot to visualize this.
```{r}
nat_trend <- lung_clean %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(mean_rate = mean(mortality_rate, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(nat_trend, aes(x = year, y = mean_rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "darkred") +
  labs(
    title = "National Lung Cancer Mortality Rate (2000–2019)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Deaths per 100,000 (Age-adjusted)"
  )
```
From this graph, we observe a downward trend of the national mortality rate. The number of death has decreased steadily from ~112 deaths per 100,000 in 2000 to ~82 deaths per 100,000 in 2019. Efforts to increase early-prevention measures such as low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screenig and better treatments over the past two decades likely contributed to this decline.

Building on the national trend, next we want to examine how mortality rates have differed between men and women over time to assess whether these overall declines have been experienced equally across sexes.

## 2. Mortality Trends By Sex
```{r}
sex_trend <- lung_clean %>%
  group_by(year, sex) %>%
  summarize(rate = mean(mortality_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(sex_trend, aes(x = year, y = rate, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Lung Cancer Mortality by Sex (2000–2019)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Deaths per 100,000",
    color = "Sex"
  )

```
In this graph, we observe that males consistently have higher mortality rates than females, with rates declining from approximately 150 to 100 deaths per 100,000. On the other hand, females experienced a slower decline, with their rates leveling off between 2005 and 2010. 

These sex-based differences are likely rooted in historical smoking behavior, as men adopted and abandoned smoking earlier than women. Additionally, early public health messaging often targeted men more aggressively, while female smoking rates rose later in the 20th century and may have plateaued at different times depending on social and cultural factors. The slower decline in female mortality could also point to gaps in screening or treatment access for women in specific age or socioeconomic groups.

In addition, we also explore how lung cancer mortality rates vary across different age groups to better understand which populations are most affected and how these trends have changed over time.
## 3. Mortality Trends By Age Group
```{r}
age_trend <- lung_clean %>%
  group_by(year, age_group) %>%
  summarize(mean_rate = mean(mortality_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(age_trend, aes(x = year, y = mean_rate, color = age_group)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Lung Cancer Mortality by Age Group",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Deaths per 100,000",
    color = "Age Group"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")


```
Looking at the pink lines, older age groups show significantly higher mortality rates, exceeding 400 deaths per 100,000. In contrast, younger groups (under 50 years) maintain low and nearly flat rates. This indicates that lung cancer predominantly affects older adults, which align with existing studies. The decline observed in older age groups likely reflects improvements in screening and treatment, as well as the cumulative impact of reduced risk factors over time. 

To understand whether and how lung cancer mortality differs across the U.S., we next examine state-level mortality rates from 2000–2019. Visualizing these trends and comparing them with environmental and behavioral risk factors (e.g., smoking prevalence, air pollution, and socioeconomic indicators) will help identify regions with persistently high rates or the greatest/least improvements over time.

From the above graphs, Kentucky, West Virginia, Maine, and Mississippi are among the states with the highest mortality rates (>120 deaths per 100,000). These states historically have high smoking prevalence and potentially limited access to healthcare, which can contribute to the higher mortality rates. Utah and Colorado show the lowest rates, likely due to lower smoking rates and stronger public health measures. These states are also known for benefit from strong public health systems, robust anti-smoking legislation, and generally healthier lifestyles. The geographic contrast suggests that state-level policy, economic conditions, and healthcare infrastructure play a substantial role in determining lung cancer outcomes.

While geographic differences highlight the influence of local policies, healthcare access, and environmental exposures, they do not fully explain the disparities in lung cancer outcomes. Race and ethnicity can also play a critical role as behavioral, gen. In the following graphs, we group our data by race and plot throughout the years to further investigate these differences.

```{r}
race_trend <- lung_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(race), race != "All Races") %>%
  group_by(year, race) %>%
  summarize(mean_rate = mean(mortality_rate, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(race_trend, aes(x = year, y = mean_rate, color = race)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +
  labs(
    title = "Lung Cancer Mortality Trends by Race Group",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Deaths per 100,000",
    color = "Race Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12)
  )
```

American Indian and Alaska Native groups have the highest lung cancer mortality rates, which increased between 2000 and 2005 before declining. Their rates rose initially between 2000 and 2005 and then gradually declined, but they remained the most impacted racial group from 2005 onward. This trend may reflect historical underinvestment in native health services, higher smoking rates, and limited access to preventive care. Furthermore, black populations started with the highest rate in 2000 but achieved significant reductions, approaching parity with other races by 2019. This progress suggests that interventions targeting smoking cessation and lung health within Black communities may have begun to take effect. In contrast, Asian Americans consistently had the lowest mortality rates, which remained stable with only minor variation. This could be attributed to lower smoking prevalence and possibly genetic or environmental factors that requires further investigation. Asian populations show relatively stable, low mortality, possibly due to lower historical smoking prevalence.

So far, we have discovered and visualized clear demographical disparities in lung cancer mortality. To further quantify and identify variables that contribute the most to mortality rate, we decided to build linear regression models. Since our response variable (mortality rate) is a continuous variable, a linear regression model fits our use case.

## Regression Analysis
```{r}

# Filter out unnecessary age groups for our model
lung_clean_filtered <- lung_clean %>%
  filter(!age_group %in% c(
    "<1 year", "1 to 4", "5 to 9", "10 to 14", "All Ages", 
    "Age-standardized"
  ))

# Convert predictors to factors since they are categorical
lung_clean_filtered$sex <- as.factor(lung_clean_filtered$sex)
lung_clean_filtered$race <- as.factor(lung_clean_filtered$race)
lung_clean_filtered$age_group <- as.factor(lung_clean_filtered$age_group)

# Explicitly setting the reference level since R will by default, choose its reference based on alphabetical order
lung_clean_filtered$age_group <- relevel(lung_clean_filtered$age_group, ref = "60 to 64")
lung_clean_filtered$sex <- relevel(lung_clean_filtered$sex, ref = "Male")
lung_clean_filtered$race <- relevel(lung_clean_filtered$race, ref = "White")
```

Here is our regression model with year, sex, race, and age group being the predictor variables, and mortality rate as response variable:
```{r}
model <- lm(mortality_rate ~ year + sex + race + age_group, data = lung_clean_filtered)

summary(model)
```
We achieved a R-squared of 0.75, which means that about 75% of the variability in mortality rate is explained by the model. All of our predictors are statistically significant (p < 0.001), meaning they all show a meaningful relationship with mortality rate. 

We also performed a regression model without year. We expect the coefficients of these variables to shift if the disparities have changed over time. 

```{r}
model_2 <- lm(mortality_rate ~ sex + race + age_group, data = lung_clean_filtered)

summary(model_2)
```
From this model, we observe that the coefficients remained identical as Model 1 (with year). This means that the effects of sex, race, and age on lung cancer mortality are relatively stable over time. From this, we learned that the gap between males and females, or between races, is not narrowing or widening significantly from 2000 to 2019. This also indicates that year affects the overall mortality trend but not on the demographic gaps.

### Interpretation of Regression Result on Model 1
- Year: Each year, lung cancer mortality rate decreases by 2.19, holding all else constant.
- Female: Females have about 78 fewer deaths per 100,000 than males, holding all else constant.
- American Indian/Alaska Native: AIAN individuals have a 13.42 units higher mortality rate than white individuals.
- Asian: Asians have a 76.82 units lower mortality rate than white individuals.
- Black: Black individuals have a 9.87 units higher mortality rate than white individuals.
- Latino: Latino individuals have a 89.85 units lower mortality rate than white individuals.
- all younger age groups below our reference level of 60-64 shows lower mortality rate, while all older age groups above our reference level shows higher mortality rate. This aligns with expectations that lung cancer risk increases with age. 

Temporal Trend: Our model shows that mortality rates are declining over time, with approximately 2.19 reduction each year.

Sex Differences:  Males continue to have a greater incidence of lung cancer compared to females, even when race, age group, and year are controlled. This observation aligns with the historical trends of lung cancer related to tobacco use; males have been more prone to smoking and occupational lung cancer risks.  

Racial Disparities: Latinos and Asians showed a significantly lower mortality rate compared to white individuals, whereas Blacks and AIAN groups have higher mortality rate compared to white individuals, holding all else constant.  
Age Effect: The pattern of the data confirms that the younger age group, controlling for other factors, contains the lowest mortality rates. On the other hand, the older age group shows higher mortality rates. This confirms the effect of a combination of biological factors and the long-term accumulation of risk factors in smoking.

## Conclusionn
In our EDA, we uncovered several patterns and disparities in lung cancer mortality in the United States from 2000 to 2019. We examined trends across time, age, sex, race, and location, and by using a multivariable linear regression model, we were able to quantify the impact of each factor while controlling for others. However, our dataset did not incorporate certain factors that could have helped further explain our results, such as smoking status, access to healthcare, and air quality. In addition to that, our data only extends to 2019 so we were unable to account for trends as a result of more recent policies. 

Our next steps will focus on expanding our analysis by adding state-level predictors into the regression model in order to gauge how mortality disparity is affected by geography. We also plan to integrate smoking prevalence, air quality, and healthcare access datasets to investigate the underlying causes of these disparities. Finally, we want to include data after 2019 to capture the effects of recent public health policies.

Ultimately, a coordinated effort combining research, policy, and community engagement is essential to shorten the lung cancer mortality gap and promote equitable health for everyone, regardless of their race, gender, or age. We look forward to building on this EDA analysis by investigating the underlying drivers of these disparities, evaluating the effectiveness of targeted interventions, and leveraging more recent and external data to achieve this.
